notes: BATCH_001 Banking and Financial Awareness part: 200 original questions (60 Basic, 80 Intermediate, 60 Advanced) across 30 topics, IDs BANK_BFA_000004 to BANK_BFA_000203. Every question carries fact checks against primary sources (RBI, NPCI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA, PIB/DFS, BIS, IBBI, exchanges) opened or search-confirmed on 2026-11-05; changeable values carry current_affairs dates. Computed answers are re-derived in tools/batch_001/banking.py. Repo Rate and Budget/Economic Survey topics are excluded.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: What is the maximum deposit insurance cover that DICGC provides to a depositor of an insured bank?

options.text: ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, for principal and interest together
₹5 lakh per account, so each account of the depositor is covered separately
₹10 lakh per depositor across all banks

solution.explanation: The Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC), a wholly owned subsidiary of RBI, insures each depositor in an insured bank up to ₹5,00,000 for principal and interest together. Deposits held in the same right and capacity in all branches of a bank are added up for this limit. The cover was raised from ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh with effect from 4 February 2020.
steps: It is per depositor per bank (all branches combined), not per account
Principal and interest are covered together within ₹5 lakh
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1 lakh was the limit before 4 February 2020. The limit is per depositor per bank, not per account, and deposits in different banks are covered separately rather than under one combined cap.
solution.final_answer: Option B: ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, for principal and interest together

fact_checks.claim: Each depositor is insured up to ₹5,00,000 for principal and interest; deposits in all branches of a bank are aggregated
DICGC raised the cover from ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh per depositor with effect from 4 February 2020

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Which of the following is a feature of a Basic Savings Bank Deposit Account (BSBDA) as prescribed by RBI?

options.text: An initial deposit of ₹1,000 is needed to open it
Only two deposits are allowed in a month
It can be opened only by persons with income below ₹1 lakh
No minimum balance needs to be maintained

solution.explanation: Under RBI's Commercial Banks – Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025 (BSBD paragraphs as amended on 4 December 2025, effective 1 April 2026), the BSBD account is a normal banking service available to all. Its facilities are free without any minimum balance, no initial deposit is needed, deposits are unlimited in number and value, and at least four free withdrawals a month are given.
steps: BSBDA is RBI's no-frills account for financial inclusion
Key feature: no minimum balance and no initial deposit
solution.why_others_wrong: No initial deposit is required; deposits are unlimited in number and value; there is no income condition.
solution.final_answer: Option D: No minimum balance needs to be maintained

fact_checks.claim: BSBD account (commercial banks, effective 1 April 2026): facilities free without any minimum balance; no initial deposit; no limit on number and value of deposits; minimum four free withdrawals a month; available to all

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A 'scheduled bank' in India is a bank that is included in:

options.text: The Second Schedule to the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934
The Third Schedule to the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
The First Schedule to the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
The Schedule to the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970

solution.explanation: Banks listed in the Second Schedule to the RBI Act, 1934 are scheduled banks. A bank qualifies if its paid-up capital and reserves are at least ₹5 lakh and RBI is satisfied that its affairs are not conducted against depositors' interests. Scheduled banks must keep CRR with RBI and can access RBI liquidity.
steps: 'Scheduled' refers to the Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934
Inclusion is under Section 42(6)(a) of the RBI Act
solution.why_others_wrong: The Third Schedule of the BR Act prescribes balance-sheet forms; the other Acts do not define scheduled status.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The Second Schedule to the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934

fact_checks.claim: Banks included in the Second Schedule to the RBI Act, 1934 are scheduled banks; criteria: paid-up capital and reserves of at least ₹5 lakh and affairs not detrimental to depositors

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: For how long from the date of issue is a cheque, draft or pay order valid for payment, as per RBI instructions?

solution.concept: Validity of cheques and bank instruments
solution.explanation: From 1 April 2012, RBI reduced the validity of cheques, drafts, pay orders and banker's cheques from six months to three months from the date of issue. An instrument presented after three months is 'stale' and is not paid.
steps: RBI circular of 4 November 2011, effective 1 April 2012
Validity = 3 months from the date of issue
solution.why_others_wrong: Six months was the validity before 1 April 2012; one month and one year were never the rule.
solution.final_answer: Option C: 3 months

fact_checks.claim: Cheques/drafts/pay orders presented beyond three months from date of issue shall not be paid (effective 1 April 2012)

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Positive Pay System for cheques, banks must enable the facility for all account holders issuing cheques of what amount?

solution.explanation: Under Positive Pay (from 1 January 2021), the drawer sends key cheque details such as date, payee and amount to the bank in advance; CTS cross-checks them when the cheque is presented. Banks must enable it for cheques of ₹50,000 and above. Using it is the customer's choice, but banks may make it mandatory for cheques of ₹5 lakh and above.
steps: ₹5 lakh is only the level at which banks MAY make it mandatory
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹5 lakh is the optional mandatory level for banks, not the threshold for enabling the facility. ₹10,000 and ₹2 lakh are not PPS thresholds.
solution.final_answer: Option D: ₹50,000 and above

fact_checks.claim: Banks to enable Positive Pay for all account holders issuing cheques of ₹50,000 and above; may make it mandatory for ₹5 lakh and above; implemented from 1 January 2021

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under 'continuous clearing and settlement on realisation' in the Cheque Truncation System (Phase 1 from 4 October 2025), what happens to a cheque that the drawee bank does not confirm within the prescribed time?

options.text: It is carried over to the next working day's clearing
It is treated as deemed approved and included in settlement
It is referred to RBI for a decision

solution.explanation: RBI moved CTS from batch clearing to continuous clearing in two phases (Phase 1 on 4 October 2025, Phase 2 announced for 3 January 2026). Cheques are scanned and presented continuously in one session; the drawee bank must confirm (positive or negative) within the prescribed window, failing which the cheque is deemed approved and settled. Settlement runs hourly, and banks credit customers within one hour of settlement.
steps: Drawee bank must send a positive or negative confirmation
No confirmation in time → deemed approved → settled
solution.why_others_wrong: An unconfirmed cheque is not returned or carried over; RBI does not decide individual cheques.
solution.final_answer: Option C: It is treated as deemed approved and included in settlement

fact_checks.claim: CTS moves to continuous clearing and settlement on realisation: Phase 1 on 4 October 2025; cheques not confirmed within the prescribed time are deemed approved
Banks are required to credit customer accounts within one hour of settlement

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Which non-resident account is maintained in Indian rupees and allows the funds in it to be repatriated abroad freely without RBI approval?

solution.explanation: An NRE account is a rupee account whose funds can be repatriated outside India without RBI approval. An NRO account is also in rupees but is meant for income earned in India, and remittance of its balances is capped. FCNR(B) deposits are held in foreign currency, not rupees.
solution.why_others_wrong: NRO is not freely repatriable; FCNR(B) is a foreign-currency account; RFC accounts are for returning residents, not non-residents.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Non-Resident External (NRE) account

fact_checks.claim: NRE account funds may be repatriated outside India without RBI approval

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: To be included in the Second Schedule to the RBI Act, a bank's paid-up capital and reserves must in aggregate be at least:

solution.explanation: Under Section 42(6)(a) of the RBI Act, a bank can be included in the Second Schedule if its paid-up capital and reserves are not less than ₹5 lakh in aggregate and RBI is satisfied that its affairs are not being conducted in a manner detrimental to the interests of its depositors.
steps: Recall the RBI Act criterion: paid-up capital + reserves ≥ ₹5 lakh
Plus RBI's satisfaction about depositor interests
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹100 crore and similar figures are licensing capital norms for new banks, not the scheduling criterion.
solution.final_answer: Option B: ₹5 lakh

fact_checks.claim: Inclusion in the Second Schedule requires paid-up capital and reserves of at least ₹5 lakh and affairs not detrimental to depositors' interests

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Who bears the deposit insurance premium payable to DICGC?

options.text: The depositor, through an annual deduction
The insured bank, which cannot pass it on to depositors

solution.explanation: Deposit insurance is mandatory for insured banks. The premium is borne entirely by the insured bank and cannot be passed on to depositors; it is paid half-yearly on the bank's assessable deposits.
steps: Premium is the bank's cost, not the depositor's
solution.why_others_wrong: Depositors pay nothing for the cover; neither the Government nor RBI pays the premium.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The insured bank, which cannot pass it on to depositors

fact_checks.claim: Deposit insurance premium is borne entirely by the insured bank and cannot be passed on to depositors

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Ravi holds, in his individual name, a savings account of ₹3.2 lakh at one branch of Bank X and a fixed deposit of ₹2.5 lakh (including interest) at another branch of Bank X. He also has a fixed deposit of ₹4 lakh in Bank Y. If Bank X goes into liquidation, how much will DICGC pay Ravi in respect of Bank X?

solution.concept: DICGC cover: per depositor, per bank, same right and capacity
solution.explanation: Deposits held in the same right and capacity in all branches of the same bank are added together: 3.2 + 2.5 = ₹5.7 lakh. The cover is capped at ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, so Ravi receives ₹5 lakh for Bank X. His deposit in Bank Y is in a separate bank and is not affected.
steps: Bank Y deposits are irrelevant to Bank X's claim
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹5.7 lakh ignores the cap; ₹9.7 lakh wrongly adds Bank Y; ₹3.2 lakh treats branches separately.
solution.final_answer: Option B: ₹5 lakh

fact_checks.claim: Each depositor insured up to ₹5,00,000; deposits in all branches of a bank held in the same capacity are aggregated

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements:
I. A cheque dated 10 January 2026 presented for payment on 15 April 2026 should not be paid by the bank.
II. A bank may collect an 'account payee' cheque into the account of a third party if the payee requests it in writing.
III. RBI requires the Positive Pay System to be used for every cheque, whatever its amount.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.concept: Cheque validity, account payee crossing and Positive Pay
solution.explanation: I is correct: a cheque is valid for three months, so a cheque dated 10 January 2026 is stale after 10 April 2026. II is wrong: account payee cheques must be collected only for the named payee (the drawer should instead withdraw the account payee mandate). III is wrong: banks must enable Positive Pay for cheques of ₹50,000 and above, and its use is at the customer's discretion.
steps: I: 10 Jan + 3 months = 10 Apr; 15 Apr is beyond → not payable (correct)
II: account payee cheques are not collected for third parties (wrong)
III: PPS is enabled for ₹50,000+ and is not compulsory for every cheque (wrong)
solution.final_answer: Option A: I only

fact_checks.claim: Instruments presented beyond three months from the date of issue shall not be paid
Account payee cheques payable to third parties should not be collected
Positive Pay to be enabled for cheques of ₹50,000 and above; availing it is at the account holder's discretion

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: In a month in 2026-27, a BSBD account holder of a commercial bank makes 3 ATM cash withdrawals, 2 cash withdrawals at the branch, 4 UPI payments and 1 NEFT transfer. Under RBI's BSBD rules in force from 1 April 2026, which statement is correct?

options.text: 10 transactions count as withdrawals and all must be free
Only the 3 ATM cash withdrawals count, so all of them must be free
5 transactions count as withdrawals and all 5 must be free because a BSBDA carries no charges
5 transactions count as withdrawals; at least 4 must be free and the bank decides on the fifth

solution.explanation: Under RBI's Commercial Banks – Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025 (BSBD paragraphs as amended on 4 December 2025, effective 1 April 2026), a BSBD account gets a minimum of four free withdrawals a month, including transfers and ATM transactions. Digital payments other than ATM transactions (POS, NEFT, RTGS, UPI, IMPS) are not counted as withdrawals. Here 3 ATM + 2 branch = 5 withdrawals: four must be free; whether the fifth is charged is the bank's decision. (Before April 2026, NEFT and other modes also counted towards the four.)
steps: UPI (4) and NEFT (1) are digital payments, not counted
Minimum free = 4; the fifth is at the bank's discretion
solution.why_others_wrong: UPI and NEFT payments are not counted as withdrawals; RBI mandates a minimum of four free, not all.
solution.final_answer: Option D: 5 transactions count as withdrawals; at least 4 must be free and the bank decides on the fifth

fact_checks.claim: BSBD (commercial banks, effective 1 April 2026): minimum four free withdrawals a month including transfers and ATM transactions; POS, NEFT, RTGS, UPI, IMPS etc. not counted as withdrawals

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: An NRI has ₹12 crore in his NRO account from the sale of inherited property and wants to remit the equivalent of USD 1.2 million abroad in the current financial year. Under the NRO rules, what is permitted?

options.text: He can remit the full USD 1.2 million because NRO funds are freely repatriable
He cannot remit anything because NRO balances are fully non-repatriable
He can remit up to USD 1 million this financial year; the balance must wait for a later year
He must first convert the NRO balance into an FCNR(B) deposit, after which there is no limit

solution.explanation: NRO balances of NRIs/PIOs can be remitted up to USD 1 million per financial year (April–March), together with other eligible assets, subject to tax and FEMA conditions. So only USD 1 million can go out this year; the remaining USD 0.2 million can be remitted in a later financial year.
steps: NRO repatriation cap: USD 1 million per financial year
Requested 1.2 million > 1 million → only 1 million this year
solution.why_others_wrong: NRO funds are not freely repatriable (that is NRE), but they are not fully blocked either. Shifting money from NRO to FCNR(B) is not a route around the cap.
solution.final_answer: Option C: He can remit up to USD 1 million this financial year; the balance must wait for a later year

fact_checks.claim: Balances in an NRO account of NRIs/PIOs are remittable up to USD 1 million per financial year (April-March)

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: How many major commercial banks were nationalised on 19 July 1969?

solution.explanation: On 19 July 1969, 14 major scheduled commercial banks, each with deposits of over ₹50 crore, were nationalised. Six more private banks were nationalised on 15 April 1980.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 is the 1980 round; 20 is the total of both rounds; 10 has no basis.
solution.final_answer: Option C: 14

fact_checks.claim: 19 July 1969: 14 major scheduled commercial banks with deposits over ₹50 crore nationalised

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: State Bank of India was constituted on 1 July 1955 by converting which bank into a state-owned institution?

solution.explanation: The Imperial Bank of India, formed in 1921 by merging the three Presidency banks, was converted into the state-owned State Bank of India on 1 July 1955.
steps: Imperial Bank of India → State Bank of India (1 July 1955)
solution.why_others_wrong: The Presidency Bank of Bombay had already merged into the Imperial Bank; Allahabad Bank merged into Indian Bank in 2020; Bank of Hindustan was an early private bank.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Imperial Bank of India

fact_checks.claim: Imperial Bank of India converted into a state-owned institution, State Bank of India, on 1 July 1955

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under the consolidation of public sector banks effective 1 April 2020, Allahabad Bank was amalgamated into:

solution.explanation: From 1 April 2020: Oriental Bank of Commerce and United Bank of India merged into Punjab National Bank; Syndicate Bank into Canara Bank; Andhra Bank and Corporation Bank into Union Bank of India; and Allahabad Bank into Indian Bank.
steps: Recall the four anchor banks and their merging partners
solution.why_others_wrong: PNB took OBC and United Bank; Union Bank took Andhra and Corporation Bank; Canara took Syndicate Bank.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Indian Bank

fact_checks.claim: Cabinet approved amalgamation w.e.f. 1.4.2020 including Allahabad Bank into Indian Bank

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under the fourth phase of RRB amalgamation based on 'One State-One RRB', effective 1 May 2025, the number of Regional Rural Banks was reduced from 43 to:

solution.explanation: The Department of Financial Services notified the amalgamation of 26 RRBs in the fourth phase, effective 1 May 2025, reducing the number of RRBs from 43 to 28. RRBs were first set up in 1975 (the first on 2 October 1975) and function under the RRBs Act, 1976.
solution.why_others_wrong: 26 is the number of RRBs amalgamated, not the number left; 30 and 33 are not the official counts.
solution.final_answer: Option B: 28

fact_checks.claim: Phase IV amalgamation of 26 RRBs; number of RRBs reduced from 43 to 28 w.e.f. 1 May 2025
28 RRBs operate; RRBs established under the RRBs Act, 1976; first RRB set up on 2 October 1975

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: The committee whose November 1991 report recommended a phased reduction of SLR and CRR and the introduction of income recognition and capital adequacy norms was chaired by:

solution.explanation: The Narasimham Committee on the Financial System (1991) laid the foundation of banking reforms: phased reduction of SLR and CRR, prudential norms for income recognition and asset classification, and capital adequacy. RBI introduced income recognition and asset classification norms in April 1992.
steps: 1991 report on the financial system → M. Narasimham
solution.why_others_wrong: Raja Chelliah headed tax reforms; Urjit Patel headed the 2014 monetary policy framework committee; Nachiket Mor headed a 2013 committee on financial services for small businesses and low-income households.
solution.final_answer: Option D: M. Narasimham

fact_checks.claim: Nov 1991: Narasimham Committee report recommended phased SLR/CRR reduction, accounting standards, income recognition and capital adequacy norms; IRAC norms introduced April 1992

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
I. Nationalisation of six private sector banks
II. Setting up of Regional Rural Banks
III. Conversion of the Imperial Bank of India into State Bank of India
IV. Establishment of NABARD

solution.explanation: Imperial Bank became SBI on 1 July 1955; RRBs were set up from 26 September 1975; six banks were nationalised on 15 April 1980; NABARD was established on 12 July 1982.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other sequences misplace the 1980 nationalisation relative to RRBs (1975) or NABARD (1982).
solution.final_answer: Option D: III, II, I, IV

fact_checks.claim: RRBs set up 26 Sep 1975; six private banks nationalised 15 Apr 1980; NABARD established 12 Jul 1982
SBI constituted 1 July 1955 from Imperial Bank of India

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements:
I. The Expert Committee chaired by Urjit R. Patel (report January 2014) recommended adopting the new CPI (combined) as the key measure of inflation.
II. The RBI Act was amended in 2016 to give a statutory basis to flexible inflation targeting.
III. Under the amended Act, the inflation target is fixed by the Monetary Policy Committee itself.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.concept: From the Urjit Patel Committee to flexible inflation targeting
solution.explanation: The Urjit Patel Committee recommended CPI (combined) as the key measure of inflation and a disinflation glide path. The RBI Act was amended in May 2016 to provide a statutory basis for flexible inflation targeting. The target itself (4% CPI, band 2–6%) is set by the Central Government in consultation with RBI, not by the MPC; the MPC sets the policy rate to achieve it.
steps: I: correct (CPI combined as key measure)
III: wrong — the Central Government sets the target
solution.final_answer: Option A: I and II only

fact_checks.claim: Urjit Patel Committee (report January 2014): recommendations included adopting CPI (combined) as the key measure of inflation
RBI Act amended in May 2016 for flexible inflation targeting; Central Government sets the 4% target with 2-6% band

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: The Reserve Bank of India was established on 1 April 1935 under which law?

solution.explanation: RBI was established on 1 April 1935 under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. It started as a privately owned bank and has been fully owned by the Government of India since nationalisation in 1949.
steps: Act passed in 1934; RBI began operations on 1 April 1935
solution.why_others_wrong: The Act is of 1934, not 1935; the BR Act, 1949 regulates banks; the GoI Act, 1935 is a constitutional statute.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934

fact_checks.claim: RBI established on April 1, 1935 under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI's central office was initially located in Kolkata (Calcutta). In which year was it permanently moved to Mumbai?

solution.explanation: The central office was set up in Kolkata in 1935 and permanently shifted to Mumbai in 1937. The Governor sits at the central office, where policy is formulated.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1935 is the year of establishment; 1949 is nationalisation; 1951 has no link.
solution.final_answer: Option B: 1937

fact_checks.claim: Central office set up in Kolkata, permanently moved to Mumbai in 1937

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Who is the Governor of the Reserve Bank of India as of November 2026?

solution.explanation: Sanjay Malhotra, an IAS officer of the 1990 Rajasthan cadre and earlier Revenue Secretary, took charge as the 26th Governor of RBI on 11 December 2024 for three years. He succeeded Shaktikanta Das and chaired the Central Board's 625th meeting on 30 October 2026.
solution.why_others_wrong: Shaktikanta Das was the previous Governor (to 10 December 2024); Poonam Gupta is a Deputy Governor; Urjit Patel was Governor in 2016–2018.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Sanjay Malhotra

fact_checks.claim: Sanjay Malhotra took charge as the 26th Governor of RBI for a three-year period effective December 11, 2024

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI was set up as a shareholders' bank. In which year was it nationalised, making it fully owned by the Government of India?

solution.explanation: RBI was privately owned when it began in 1935. It was nationalised in 1949 and has since been fully owned by the Government of India.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1947 is Independence; 1955 is the creation of SBI; 1969 is the nationalisation of 14 commercial banks.
solution.final_answer: Option D: 1949

fact_checks.claim: RBI was initially privately owned; since nationalisation in 1949 it is fully owned by the Government of India

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Apart from the Governor, how many Deputy Governors at most can be official directors on RBI's Central Board?

solution.explanation: The official directors on RBI's Central Board are the full-time Governor and not more than four Deputy Governors. Non-official directors are nominated by the Government (ten from various fields, four from the local boards, and two government officials).
steps: Official directors = Governor + up to 4 Deputy Governors
solution.why_others_wrong: RBI's structure provides for up to four Deputy Governors.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Four

fact_checks.claim: Official directors: Governor and not more than four Deputy Governors (full-time)

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a wholly owned subsidiary of RBI?

options.text: National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD)
Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC)
Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran Private Limited (BRBNMPL)

solution.explanation: RBI's fully owned subsidiaries are DICGC, BRBNMPL, ReBIT, IFTAS and RBIH. NABARD is a statutory development bank established in 1982 under its own Act and is not listed as an RBI subsidiary.
steps: List RBI subsidiaries: DICGC, BRBNMPL, ReBIT, IFTAS, RBIH
solution.why_others_wrong: DICGC, BRBNMPL and RBIH are all listed by RBI as fully owned subsidiaries.
solution.final_answer: Option A: National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD)

fact_checks.claim: RBI's fully owned subsidiaries: DICGC, BRBNMPL, ReBIT, IFTAS and RBIH

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about RBI's accounting year:
I. From 2020-21, RBI changed its accounting year from July–June to April–March.
II. The year 2020-21 was a transition year covering only nine months (July 2020 to March 2021).
III. The change was meant to align RBI's year with the Government's fiscal year.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.explanation: On the recommendation of the Expert Committee on the Economic Capital Framework (chaired by Bimal Jalan), RBI moved from a July–June to an April–March year from 2020-21, in sync with the Government's fiscal year. The transition year 2020-21 ran from July 2020 to March 2021, i.e. nine months.
solution.final_answer: Option D: I, II and III

fact_checks.claim: RBI's accounting year changed from July-June to April-March from 2020-21 on the Bimal Jalan committee's recommendation; 2020-21 covered nine months

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about the RBI Governor's roles:
I. The Governor chairs the Monetary Policy Committee and has a second or casting vote in case of a tie.
II. The Governor chairs the Sub-Committee of the Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC).
III. The Governor chairs the FSDC itself.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.explanation: The Governor is the ex-officio chairperson of the MPC and has a casting vote if votes are equal. The FSDC is chaired by the Union Finance Minister; its Sub-Committee, the primary operating arm, is chaired by the RBI Governor.
steps: II: correct (FSDC Sub-Committee chaired by Governor)
III: wrong (FSDC chaired by the Finance Minister)
solution.final_answer: Option B: I and II only

fact_checks.claim: Each MPC member has one vote; in case of equality the Governor has a second or casting vote
FSDC is chaired by the Union Finance Minister; its Sub-Committee is chaired by the RBI Governor

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI's Central Board consists of the Governor, Deputy Governors (at most four), one director from each of the four local boards, ten directors nominated by the Government from various fields and two Government officials. What is the maximum strength of the Central Board?

solution.explanation: Adding the maximum in each category: 1 Governor + 4 Deputy Governors + 4 local-board directors + 10 nominated directors + 2 Government officials = 21.
solution.why_others_wrong: 17 omits the Deputy Governors; 19 omits the Government officials; 20 drops one category member.
solution.final_answer: Option D: 21

fact_checks.claim: Central Board: Governor and up to four Deputy Governors; ten government-nominated directors, two government officials and four directors, one each from the four local boards

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI manages foreign exchange in India under which Act?

solution.concept: RBI as manager of foreign exchange
solution.explanation: RBI manages foreign exchange under FEMA, 1999, which replaced FERA, 1973 and became operative in June 2000 with the aim of facilitating external trade and payments.
solution.why_others_wrong: FERA was repealed; PMLA deals with money laundering; the BR Act regulates banking companies.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999

fact_checks.claim: RBI manages foreign exchange under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999
FEMA replaced FERA, 1973 and became operative in June 2000

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under which law are coins issued in India?

solution.concept: Issue of coins versus bank notes
solution.explanation: Bank notes are issued by RBI under the RBI Act, 1934, while coins (and one-rupee notes) are issued under the Coinage Act, 2011 by the Government of India and put into circulation through RBI. One-rupee notes issued under the Coinage Act are legal tender and treated as rupee coin.
solution.why_others_wrong: Section 22 of the RBI Act covers bank notes; the 1906 Act was replaced by the 2011 Act; the BR Act is unrelated.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The Coinage Act, 2011

fact_checks.claim: The statutory provisions for issue of bank notes and coins are the RBI Act, 1934 and the Coinage Act, 2011

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: What are Ways and Means Advances (WMA) given by RBI to the governments?

options.text: Long-term loans to finance capital expenditure
Grants to state governments for welfare schemes
Temporary advances to bridge mismatches between receipts and payments
Refinance to banks for priority sector lending

The decision is referred to the Central Government

The SDF rate is always fixed at 3.35%

options.text: Yes; inflation was above 6% in four of the five quarters
Yes; any single quarter above 6% is a failure
No; inflation stayed above 6% for at most two consecutive quarters
No; failure arises only if inflation exceeds 8%

solution.concept: Definition of failure to meet the target
solution.explanation: Failure means average inflation above the upper tolerance level (6%) or below the lower level (2%) for any three consecutive quarters. Here the run above 6% is 6.4, 6.1 (two quarters), broken by 5.8, followed by 6.5, 6.2 (two quarters). There is no run of three, so there is no failure. As standard, because farm loans become NPA only after two crop seasons
As standard until it is overdue for more than 90 days from the next harvest
As a loss asset, because agricultural loans are unsecured

questions.question_text: A loan of ₹100 lakh has been in the doubtful category for two years. The realisable value of the security is ₹70 lakh. Under RBI's current provisioning norms (Directions, 2025), what is the minimum provision required?

solution.explanation: For doubtful assets, the unsecured portion (not covered by the realisable value of security) needs 100% provision. The secured portion needs 25% (doubtful up to 1 year), 40% (1–3 years) or 100% (over 3 years). Unsecured = 100 − 70 = 30 → ₹30 lakh. Secured (doubtful for 2 years) = 70 × 40% = ₹28 lakh. Total = ₹58 lakh. Note: from 1 April 2027 these norms are replaced by RBI's expected credit loss framework.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹28 lakh ignores the unsecured portion; ₹40 lakh applies 40% to the whole loan; ₹100 lakh treats it as a loss asset.
solution.final_answer: Option C: ₹58 lakh

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness

options.text: High-quality liquid assets ÷ net cash outflows over 30 days; at least 100%
Tier 1 capital ÷ total exposure; at least 3.5%
Available stable funding ÷ total deposits; at least 75%
Available stable funding ÷ required stable funding; at least 100%

solution.explanation: NSFR = available stable funding ÷ required stable funding, to be at least 100% on an ongoing basis. It promotes stable funding over a one-year horizon; RBI's NSFR guidelines took effect on 1 October 2021. The LCR, by contrast, compares HQLA with 30-day net cash outflows.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A scheduled commercial bank (not a D-SIB) has CET1 capital of ₹600 crore, Additional Tier 1 of ₹100 crore, Tier 2 of ₹200 crore and risk-weighted assets of ₹8,000 crore. Which statement is correct?

CRAR is 11.25%, which is short of the 11.5% required including CCB

solution.explanation: The beneficiary bank must credit the beneficiary's account within 30 minutes of receiving the RTGS message. If it cannot, it must return the funds within one hour of receipt or before the end of the RTGS business day, whichever is earlier.
steps: If not possible: return within 1 hour
solution.why_others_wrong: Two hours is the NEFT timeline; one hour is the return window, not the credit window.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A customer wants to send three separate payments of ₹1.5 lakh, ₹3 lakh and ₹7 lakh through RTGS. Which statement is correct?

options.text: All three can go through RTGS; total charges can be at most ₹75 plus tax
The ₹1.5 lakh payment cannot go through RTGS; outward charges on the other two can be at most ₹75 plus tax
The ₹1.5 lakh payment cannot go through RTGS; the other two must be free because RTGS is 24x7
All three can go through RTGS and each can be charged up to ₹50 plus tax

solution.explanation: RTGS has a minimum of ₹2 lakh, so ₹1.5 lakh must use NEFT or IMPS. Outward RTGS charges are capped at ₹25 for ₹2–5 lakh and ₹50 above ₹5 lakh (excluding tax); inward RTGS is free. So the ₹3 lakh and ₹7 lakh payments can cost at most 25 + 50 = ₹75 plus tax.
solution.why_others_wrong: The ₹1.5 lakh payment is below the minimum; 24x7 availability does not make outward RTGS free; the ₹50 cap applies only above ₹5 lakh.
solution.final_answer: Option B: The ₹1.5 lakh payment cannot go through RTGS; outward charges on the other two can be at most ₹75 plus tax

fact_checks.claim: RTGS minimum ₹2,00,000; outward charges up to ₹25 (₹2-5 lakh) and ₹50 (above ₹5 lakh) excluding tax; inward free

Accepting savings and current account deposits

solution.explanation: Since payments banks cannot lend, the 2014 licensing guidelines required them to invest at least 75% of their demand deposit balances in SLR-eligible government securities or T-bills with maturity up to one year, and allowed at most 25% in current and time deposits with other scheduled commercial banks.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A customer of a payments bank has a balance of ₹1.8 lakh and receives a credit of ₹50,000 during the day. What must the payments bank ensure?

options.text: Not more than ₹2 lakh remains at the end of the day; the excess may be swept to a partner bank account with the customer's prior consent
It must reject the ₹50,000 credit, because the balance can never exceed ₹2 lakh even during the day
It can keep ₹2.3 lakh, because the limit applies only to savings accounts opened after 2021
It must convert the excess into a fixed deposit with the payments bank

solution.explanation: The ₹2 lakh limit applies to the balance at the end of the day, not to intraday credits. 1.8 + 0.5 = ₹2.3 lakh, so ₹30,000 cannot stay overnight. A payments bank may act as a BC of another bank and, with the customer's prior written consent, sweep the excess into the customer's account with that bank. Payments banks cannot accept term deposits, so a fixed deposit is not possible.
steps: End-of-day balance would be ₹2.3 lakh > ₹2 lakh
Excess ₹30,000 must leave by end of day
Route: sweep to partner bank with prior consent
solution.why_others_wrong: The cap is an end-of-day limit, applies to all individual customers, and payments banks cannot take fixed deposits.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Not more than ₹2 lakh remains at the end of the day; the excess may be swept to a partner bank account with the customer's prior consent

questions.question_text: A 91-day Treasury Bill with a face value of ₹100 is bought at ₹98.50 and held to maturity. What is the annualised yield (approx.), using a 365-day year?

solution.explanation: Return = face value − price = ₹1.50 over 91 days on an investment of ₹98.50. Yield = (1.50 ÷ 98.50) × (365 ÷ 91) × 100 ≈ 6.11%. Dividing by the face value instead of the price gives the discount rate (≈ 6.02%), which understates the investor's yield.
